newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends firmer in quiet U.S., above 116 yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends firmer in quiet U.S., above 116 yen.

text.p: The dollar ended higher against the yen on Monday partly as traders noticed Japanese officials failed to make public comments aimed at limiting the latest gains in the U.S. currency, experts said.
"Part of it is the fact that no Japanese official voiced any kind of concern about the dollar being higher overnight," said David Gilmore, a partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
"In a sense, it seems that perhaps maybe the weak economy is forcing the Japanese goverment to back down from its 115 perceived ceiling," Gilmore added.

After the dollar had climbed briefly above 115 yen last Thursday, a senior official from Japan's Ministry of Finance had warned that Japanese monetary authorities do not welcome wild fluctuations in foreign exchange rates. A Bank of Japan official had also said the central bank was carefully monitoring developments in the foreign exchange market.
Since then, the dollar has repeatedly surged above 116 yen, but neither finance ministry or central bank officials have made any objections.
The dollar hit 116.20 yen on Friday, its highest level in 45 months, and nearly scaled that peak again on Monday.

The dollar closed at 116.12/17 yen, up from 115.95/00 yen at the open. The dollar has not closed above the 116 yen threshold since it closed at 116.45 yen during the week of March 28, 1993. Against the German currency, the dollar fell slightly to 1.5545/55 marks from 1.5565/75 at the open.
Further dollar gains versus the yen are possible if monetary officials in both Japan or the U.S. remain silent.

If we don't have that type of comment or maybe even just an implied comment like that from either side, I think the dollar's definitely got some room to go higher," said Elliott Dix, an assistant vice president at Signet Bank.
Dix said the only factor holding the dollar back is expected government opposition on either side of the Pacific to a stronger dollar.

A lingering slump in Tokyo stocks also helped boost the dollar relative to the yen on Monday. Tokyo's Nikkei 225 finished the last trading day of the year at 19,361.35, down 7.69 points from Friday's close. Financial markets in Japan will resume trading on January 6 after the New Year holiday.
"The weak Nikkei, it's a real problem because the banks value their capital based on the stock prices because they own a lot of equity," Gilmore said.
"It undermines the fiscal position(s) of the institutions and the industry, and that's not a good sign," said Gilmore, adding it will keep pressure on Japanese interest rates.

Trading was very light on Monday ahead of the New Year holiday on Wednesday. United States financial markets close early on Tuesday and will remain closed Wednesday. Some European markets will close on Tuesday as well as Wednesday.

Elsewhere, the dollar ended at 1.3482/92 Swiss francs, down from 1.3519/24 francs at the open. Sterling inched up to $1.6900/10 from $1.6883/93. The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3699/04 from C$1.3678/83.
The Australian dollar finished at $0.7961/68, little changed from $0.7965/70.
